title: Time, Place and Manner
short: In public forums, content-neutral rules on time, place and manner are valid if narrowly tailored to a significant government interest and leaving open ample alternative channels (Ward v. Rock Against Racism, 1989); they need not be the least restrictive means.
trouble: Students apply strict scrutiny's "least restrictive means" to these rules. Ward says a time, place and manner rule need not be the least restrictive means.

blocks.html: Note: This is an educational course, not legal advice.

In a public forum, government may still set content-neutral rules about when, where and how people speak: no sound trucks at midnight, no marches through a hospital zone, permits for big rallies. These are time, place and manner rules.

opts.facts: New York City required concerts at the Central Park bandshell to use the city's sound system and sound technician, to control volume for nearby residents and the park's quieter areas. A group that sponsored rock concerts challenged the rule.
opts.test: A content-neutral time, place or manner rule is valid if it is narrowly tailored to serve a significant government interest and leaves open ample alternative channels for communication.
opts.reasoning: Justice Kennedy wrote that narrow tailoring here does not mean the least restrictive or least intrusive means: the rule is valid if the interest would be achieved less effectively without it and it does not burden substantially more speech than necessary.

head: Requirement
Question
Ward
rows: Does the rule apply without regard to the message?
yes: protecting residents and park users from excessive noise
Does it avoid burdening substantially more speech than needed? (Not least restrictive means)
yes: the city mixed sound to the group's wishes, controlling only volume
Can the speaker still reach the audience?

blocks.html: Why a gentler standard than strict scrutiny? Because these rules do not pick sides or topics; they manage shared spaces so many people can use them. Courts still check that the rule is really neutral and not too broad. In Clark v. Community for Creative Non-Violence (1984), a ban on sleeping in a park near the White House was upheld, even for protesters sleeping to call attention to homelessness. In Frisby v. Schultz (1988) a ban on picketing focused on a single residence was upheld to protect the home.

A content-neutral time, place or manner rule is valid if narrowly tailored to a significant interest and leaving ample alternative channels (Ward v. Rock Against Racism (1989)). It need not be the least restrictive means.

blocks.title: A noise rule
blocks.q: A city limits amplified sound in a downtown plaza to 70 decibels from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m., and bans it otherwise. A street preacher challenges it. Analysis?
steps: Content-neutral: it applies to all amplified sound.
Significant interest: noise control for residents and businesses.
Narrowly tailored: it regulates volume and hours, not speech itself, and speakers can still talk without amplification or use it during the day.

blocks.title: A neutral rule that is too broad
blocks.q: A town bans all leafleting everywhere in town to prevent litter. Valid?
steps: But a total ban burdens far more speech than needed to prevent litter; the town could punish littering itself.
The Court has long struck down such bans (Schneider v. State, 1939).

blocks.html: Applying strict scrutiny's "least restrictive means" to these rules. Ward says a time, place and manner rule need not be the least restrictive means; it fails only if it burdens substantially more speech than necessary.
